name: Misinterpreted-effort hypothesis
aliases: Effort as a cue for poor learning
statement: Learners read the mental effort a study method costs as a sign it is teaching them little, rate it as the weaker method, and choose the easier one instead.
meaning: The claim is a chain of three links, not a single feeling. Effort experienced during study lowers the judgment of how much was learned; that judgment lowers the rated effectiveness of the strategy; the rating decides which strategy gets used next. Kirk-Johnson, Galla and Fraundorf named it in 2019 and tested it by mediation, so the specific prediction is that effort acts on choice through perceived learning rather than beside it. That distinguishes it from a simpler story in which people dodge hard work because it is hard. They call the simpler story the effort-avoidance hypothesis, and it predicts a direct path from effort to choice with perceived learning left out. The two make different predictions about a learner who is told which strategy works. Under effort avoidance the learner knows and declines. Under misinterpreted effort the learner does not know, because the effort has already been read as failure.

origin.who: Afton Kirk-Johnson, Brian M. Galla and Scott H. Fraundorf
origin.note: Their paper is "Perceiving effort as poor learning: The misinterpreted-effort hypothesis of how experienced effort and perceived learning relate to study strategy choice", volume 115, article 101237. Its full text is closed at every location OpenAlex and Unpaywall list and was not obtained for this entry, so what appears below comes from its abstract, read at PubMed and again through the Semantic Scholar API, and from later papers describing it.

evidence: The 2019 abstract reports four studies. Learners experienced a pair of contrasting strategies, interleaved against blocked schedules in Study 1 and retrieval practice against restudy in Studies 2 and 3, rated each, then chose one for future use. In all three, mediation showed that participants who found a strategy more effortful rated it less effective and were then less likely to choose it, and in Study 3 choosing the more effortful strategy went with better long-term retention. Study 4 indicated the pattern was not produced by the act of rating. Macaluso, Beuford and Fraundorf ran the paradigm again with added measures of familiarity. In Study 1, 328 undergraduates learned to tell bird families apart under both schedules. They rated interleaving more effortful, 3.73 against 3.10 on a six-point composite, t(327) = 10.04, p < .001, d = 0.55, and less effective for learning, 2.84 against 3.45, t(327) = -8.53, p < .001, d = -0.47. Blocking was chosen by 76.6%. The mediation held: the more effortful interleaving felt, the less learning was perceived, t = -11.31, p < .001, and the less often it was chosen, with an indirect effect of z = -4.61, p < .001 and a direct effect of z = 0.03, p = .97. Study 2 repeated this with 377 undergraduates and added a post-test. Blocking was chosen by 76.9%, and the post-test went the other way, 60% of exemplars classified correctly after interleaving against 55% after blocking, t(376) = 3.44, p < .001, d = 0.18. Janssen and colleagues measured effort directly with the nine-point Paas scale in two experiments on Dutch students recruited through Prolific. In Experiment 1, 150 students learned ten painters under both schedules. Interleaving was rated 6.26 against 3.97 for effort, t(149) = -21.93, p < 0.001, d = -1.79, drew lower concurrent judgments of learning, 3.96 against 6.18, t(149) = 20.64, p < 0.001, d = 1.69, and lower predicted test scores, 3.52 against 5.31, t(149) = 11.05, p < 0.001, d = 0.90, while producing higher actual scores, 4.83 against 3.70, t(149) = -6.36, p < 0.001, d = -0.52. Path models put effort on perceived effectiveness both directly and through predicted scores for interleaving, and only through predicted scores for blocking. Onan, Wiradhany, Biwer, Janssen and de Bruin tracked the same ratings over time in 150 Prolific undergraduates learning painting styles. Effort ratings for interleaving fell across study units as perceived learning rose, and the fall predicted choosing it, B = -3.64, 95% CI [-5.72, -1.74], with the effect running entirely through perceived learning once that was controlled, B = 0.35, 95% CI [-2.15, 2.89]. Interleaving was the habitual strategy of 13% of them before the session and the choice of 40% after it.

replication.headline: Macaluso, Beuford and Fraundorf reproduced the mediation in two samples, and Janssen and colleagues found the same chain with effort measured on a standard load scale rather than inferred from a contrast.
replication.detail: Macaluso and colleagues describe their design as an adaptation of the 2019 paradigm, using its bird images and taking its effort and perceived-learning items verbatim. Both of their studies recovered the mediation, in Study 1 at t = -11.31 for the effort to perceived-learning path and an indirect effect of z = -4.61, and in Study 2 at t = -11.56 and z = -5.72, with the direct path from effort to choice not reaching significance in either. Janssen and colleagues tested the chain a different way, measuring the absolute amount of effort each strategy cost rather than the difference between them, and separating the two strategies rather than pooling them. Their Experiment 2 moved study strategy between subjects, 299 students in four cells, and the direct path from effort to perceived effectiveness of interleaving disappeared there while the indirect path through predicted test scores survived. They read that as effort mattering more as a cue when a learner has both experiences to compare. Their feedback intervention, which showed each student their own effort ratings against their own test score, raised ratings of interleaving, beta = 0.24, t(296) = 3.82, p < 0.001, without overturning the preference for blocking. Fralick and Yan tried to break the chain by reframing the effort. Their abstract reports that in the effort-as-invested condition more perceived effort went with higher perceived learning and more interleaving, reversing the usual sign, and that the reframing still left only 17% choosing to interleave. They conclude the hypothesis cannot fully account for the preference for blocking.

study.cite: Macaluso, J. A., Beuford, R. R., & Fraundorf, S. H. (2022). Familiar strategies feel fluent: The role of study strategy familiarity in the misinterpreted-effort model of self-regulated learning. Journal of Intelligence, 10(4), 83.

limits: The mediation is correlational in every study located here. Effort is measured, not assigned, so the chain is consistent with a third variable driving both the effort rating and the judgment of learning. Fralick and Yan is the one attempt found to manipulate the reading of effort rather than observe it, and choice did not move. The effort gap itself is not general across tasks. Janssen and colleagues report that studies using problem-solving, troubleshooting and reasoning tasks found no effort difference between interleaved and blocked study, while category-learning studies did, and note that the null results came from between-subjects designs. Every study quoted here uses category learning from images, birds or paintings, with online adult samples and tests taken in the same session. Macaluso and colleagues state that the 2019 studies did not measure whether interleaving improved learning of their materials, which is why their own post-test matters and why its advantage, d = 0.18, is worth holding next to the 76.9% who chose blocking. Kirk-Johnson, Galla and Fraundorf's own numbers are absent from this page because the paper is paywalled; the searches covered Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC and the open web, and the author copy indexed at the University of Pittsburgh could not be reached from this machine. Fralick and Yan is paywalled too and is quoted here from its abstract alone, so no sample size or interval appears for it. No multi-site or registered replication of the hypothesis was located in those same searches.
misreadings: The Harvard active-learning study is often given as the source, and it is neither the source nor a test of the mechanism. Deslauriers, McCarty, Miller, Callaghan and Kestin published in the same year and did write that students take the increased cognitive effort of active learning to signify poorer learning. The variable their regression actually used was agreement with the statement "The instructor was effective at teaching", which they treat as a measure of perceived fluency, and their effort account rests on interviews with 17 students and on the disfluency literature. No effort rating appears in the results text, and the four survey items are printed inside a figure this entry could not read. That study is covered in this atlas under the illusion of learning, which is the wider claim that fluency inflates judgments of learning. This entry is the narrower one: the cue is felt effort, the outcome is a strategy the learner picks, and the evidence is a mediation model. A second error is to treat the hypothesis as saying people are lazy. Kirk-Johnson, Galla and Fraundorf set that up as the rival account, effort avoidance, and Macaluso and colleagues report they found only patchy support for it, in retrospective ratings and in two of three studies, while the indirect path held throughout. A third is to assume effort always marks the better method. It marks the better method in these category-learning tasks and not in the problem-solving tasks Janssen and colleagues cite, and a learner who applied the rule in reverse would be no better calibrated.
